match.reason: None of the bank points teach patient rights and responsibilities such as privacy, confidentiality and data sharing; they cover health literacy, community resources, health promotion and health as dynamic and subjective, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Rights and responsibilities in health care
card: Privacy
a patient has a right to have their personal information protected from people who have no need to see it.
Confidentiality
a health professional should keep what a patient tells them private. They share it only in limited cases, such as with the patient's consent or where the law requires it.
Information
a patient has a right to know how their health data is stored and who it may be shared with.
Responsibilities
patients have duties too, such as giving honest and complete information, so the professional can give safe and suitable care.
draft.remember: Patients have rights to privacy and information, and a duty to be honest with their carers.

a.q: Which is a responsibility of a patient rather than a right?
opts: Giving honest information about their symptoms
Knowing how their health records are stored
Having their personal details kept private
Expecting a clinic to keep what they say confidential
a.why: Giving honest information is a duty the patient carries, so the professional can give safe care. The other options are rights: privacy, confidentiality and knowing how data is stored.
a.clue: Which one is something the patient must do, not something they receive?

b.q: Sam, 17, asks his doctor's clinic how his test results are stored and who can see them. Which right is he using?
opts: The right to know how his health data is stored and shared
The right to give the clinic false information
The right to skip appointments without telling anyone
The right to see every other patient's records
b.why: Sam is asking how his data is stored and shared, which is the right to information about his own health data. The right to privacy protects his details, so it does not give him access to other patients' records.
b.clue: He is asking about his own results and who can see them.

a.best: Giving honest information about their symptoms

b.best: The right to know how his health data is stored and shared

problems.detail: The three distractors (seeing every other patient's records, skipping appointments without telling anyone, giving false information) are plainly absurd as rights. A Year 11 student can pick the answer without knowing the idea, and the right option also repeats the card's wording almost exactly.

'Honest with their carers' is confusing. In Australian health contexts 'carers' usually means family or unpaid carers, not health professionals, so students may misread whom the duty is owed to. 'Health professionals' would match the card.

check.summary: Facts are sound and both answers are clear. However, question b's distractors are absurd, so it can be answered without knowing the idea, and the remember line's 'carers' could be misread as family carers rather than health professionals.
